claims.text: Pristine SiO2 conducts heat primarily through lattice phonons and has minimal electronic thermal conductivity.
Controlled nanoscale SRO precipitates can be incorporated into an SiO2 matrix.
Incorporating controlled SRO precipitates into SiO2 will reduce its lattice thermal conductivity relative to pristine SiO2.
A periodic or otherwise optimized distribution of nanoscale SRO precipitates can be engineered in SiO2.
The lattice contribution to thermal transport dominates in the proposed SiO2 system at room temperature or the selected operating temperatures.
Nanoscale SRO precipitates act as phonon-scattering centers within SiO2.
SRO precipitates provide additional phonon-scattering sites.
The additional scattering sites reduce phonon scattering time and phonon mean free path.
Reducing phonon scattering time and mean free path lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
Modified SiO2 containing the engineered precipitates will show a measurable decrease in lattice thermal conductivity relative to pristine SiO2.
Precipitate size, density, and spatial distribution control the effectiveness of phonon scattering.
Significant deviation from an optimal precipitate configuration diminishes phonon-scattering effectiveness.
Excessive precipitate formation could cause microstructural instability in the SiO2 matrix.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity reduction depends on precipitate characteristics and their integration into the SiO2 matrix.
TEM or SEM can characterize the precipitate distribution in the proposed samples.
Laser-flash analysis or time-domain thermoreflectance can measure the relevant lattice thermal conductivity.
